progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: C03 (H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O, spectators, about −57 kJ/mol per mole of water, q = mcΔT with the total mass, ΔH = −q/n(H₂O), rounding to ΔT's significant figures, "acids that only partly split can give different values, and they get their own video"). C05 (strong and weak acids, most weak-acid molecules stay whole, the equilibrium arrow; ethanoic acid and HF are weak; ammonia is a weak base). C06 (NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻). C01 (H⁺(aq) is H₃O⁺). Module 5: Le Chatelier's principle (removing a product shifts the equilibrium right); chem-m5-c11 (dissolving: separating ions costs energy, hydration releases it, the sum sets the sign); chem-m5-c10 (Ka named, bigger Ka stronger). Year 11 Module 4: Hess's law, exothermic and endothermic, ΔH sign. Not assumed: pKa, Ka × Kb (chem-m6-c10), entropy beyond Module 5 C11's "spreading out".
progression.startsWith: Compare measured heats for strong and weak reactants. The video opens: Here's a prediction to make. Mix one mole per litre hydrochloric acid with the same amount of sodium hydroxide, and you get about minus fifty seven kilojoules per mole of water. Now swap in ethanoic acid, a weak acid.
progression.stopsAfter: explaining with particles why a weak acid still reacts completely with hydroxide; writing the enthalpy of neutralisation of a weak acid or base as the ionisation step plus about −57 kJ/mol; explaining why the ionisation step can absorb or release energy (bond breaking against water surrounding the new ions); explaining the ethanoic acid, hydrofluoric acid and ammonia values; calculating an ionisation step from measured data with the right sign; explaining why neutralisation heat cannot rank acid strength. No new calorimetry method (chem-m6-c03), no practical error analysis (chem-m6-p02), no Ka or pKa comparisons (chem-m6-c10), no weak acid with weak base.
progression.nextLesson: what Ka and pKa say about acid strength (route chem-m6-c10).

teaching.task: Swap hydrochloric acid for a weak acid in a neutralisation and you might expect less heat. Ethanoic acid gives almost the same heat, and hydrofluoric acid gives more. What really decides the heat a weak acid releases?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) ethanoic acid gives almost the same heat as HCl, and HF gives more: what decides the heat? (1); (2) a strong acid's hydrogen ions are already free, so only H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O happens (C03); a weak acid's protons are mostly still on whole molecules (C05) (2); (3) hydroxide removes the few hydronium ions, the equilibrium shifts right, more molecules ionise, until all have reacted: one extra step, not an incomplete reaction (3); (4) Hess's law: total = ionisation step + water step (about −57), so the difference is all in step one (4); (5) step one has energy in (a bond breaks) and energy out (water surrounds the new ions), so its sign varies (5); (6) ethanoic acid: the two nearly cancel, about −56 (6); (7) HF: the small fluoride ion holds water tightly, more out than in, about −68; still weak (7); (8) ammonia: its step takes energy in, about −52 (8); (9) so heat does not rank strength: methanoic acid is ten times stronger but gives the same heat; use pH or Ka (9); memory aid (10); two attempts and brief feedback (11 to 14); decision rule and handoff (15); key notes (16).
teaching.conversationalApproach: one surprise carries the video: swap hydrochloric acid for a weak acid and most people predict less heat, but ethanoic acid gives almost the same and hydrofluoric acid gives more. The particle lens shows that a weak acid still reacts completely (hydroxide removes hydronium, the equilibrium shifts right), Hess's law splits the heat into an ionisation step plus the water step of about −57 kJ/mol, and the energy ledger shows why that first step can absorb or release energy. Ethanoic acid, hydrofluoric acid and ammonia are then explained on the same staircase, and methanoic acid shows that heat cannot rank strength. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: Here's a prediction to make. Mix one mole per litre hydrochloric acid with the same amount of sodium hydroxide, and you get about minus fifty seven kilojoules per mole of water. Now swap in ethanoic acid, a weak acid. Most people predict much less heat. The measured value is about minus fifty six, almost the same. And hydrofluoric acid, also weak, gives about minus sixty eight: more heat, not less. So what really decides the heat?
teaching.understandingCheck: (A1) "50.0 mL of 1.00 mol/L ethanoic acid is mixed with 50.0 mL of 1.00 mol/L sodium hydroxide solution in a polystyrene cup. The temperature rises by 6.7 °C. Under the same conditions, the enthalpy of neutralisation of hydrochloric acid is −57 kJ/mol. Assume the density of the mixture is 1.00 g/mL and its specific heat capacity is 4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹. (a) Calculate the enthalpy of neutralisation of ethanoic acid. (b) Calculate the enthalpy change for the ionisation of ethanoic acid, and comment on its size." Scenes 4 and 6 give the model and the ethanoic acid value in words only; the calculation from data is new. Crossed mistake: "−57 − (−56) = −1 kJ/mol" (subtraction the wrong way round). (A2) "Hydrogen cyanide, HCN, is a weak acid. Its ionisation, HCN(aq) → H⁺(aq) + CN⁻(aq), absorbs about 45 kJ/mol. Using −57 kJ/mol for H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l), predict the enthalpy of neutralisation of hydrogen cyanide by sodium hydroxide, and explain why it differs from that of hydrochloric acid." New acid with a large endothermic step (the video's acids are near zero and negative; its endothermic case is a base). Crossed mistake: "−57 − 45 = −102 kJ/mol" (absorbed energy counted as released).
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017), as printed: "conduct a practical investigation to measure the enthalpy of neutralisation (ACSCH093)" "model neutralisation of strong and weak acids and bases using a variety of media" this video starts from measured enthalpies of neutralisation for strong and weak reactants and stops at a particle and energy model of the extra ionisation step. It teaches: the surprise that weak acids do not simply give less heat (ethanoic acid about the same as a strong acid, hydrofluoric acid more); that a weak acid still reacts completely, because hydroxide removes hydronium and the acid's equilibrium shifts right (Module 5 Le Chatelier callback); the two-step energy count by Hess's law (Year 11 callback): ionisation step plus the water step of about −57 kJ/mol; why the ionisation step can absorb or release energy (a bond breaks, energy in; water surrounds the new ions, energy out; Module 5 C11 callback); three cases (ethanoic acid close to zero, HF negative, ammonia positive); why neutralisation heat cannot rank acid strength. Not here: the calorimetry method and q = mcΔT taught again (chem-m6-c03; used once in attempt 1 as application, with every assumption on screen); the practical and its errors (chem-m6-p02); Ka and pKa as strength measures (chem-m6-c10, the next video; named only in scene 9); entropy as the reason HF is weak despite releasing heat (author note e; not voiced beyond one clause); weak acid with weak base (site card 3 values are wrong, see corrections); titration curves (chem-m6-c14).

design.visualSystem: Explainer engine: warm paper stage, handwritten Caveat headings, amber doodle layer. Colour key on screen throughout: H₃O⁺ teal token on pale blue water (C01); OH⁻ violet; whole weak acid molecules amber-outlined (C05, C08); the acid's anion grey-violet; spectator ions grey; water pale blue; heat warm orange ripples (C03); energy in a warm red arrow or bar pointing up, energy out a cool blue arrow or bar pointing down (M5 C11 ledger, blue here so it never clashes with teal hydronium); temperature readouts amber digits. Board layout (constant, C03 and C08): top-left the short question line; the centre holds the lens, the staircase or the bar chart, one at a time; a plate sits small at the left only when it carries the explanation. Clutter rule: at most three text items bright at once; every label fades when its sentence ends. The staircase counts as one item; only its current arrow and its label are bright. Reuse: painted plates (inspected 20 Oct): `m6-foam-cup-calorimeter-v1.png` (white lidded foam cup with a cutaway window, clear liquid, steel probe through a bung; no readout, so a coded readout chip sits on the probe top; scenes 1, 11 and the handoff), `m6-vinegar-bottle-v1.png` (plain glass bottle of pale amber vinegar, wooden-look cap, no label; scene 2, small, coded label "ethanoic (acetic) acid"), `m5x-ammonia-bottle-v1.png` (scene 8, coded label "ammonia solution"). HF and HCN have no plates on purpose: they appear as data cards with a small grey tag "data from careful lab measurements" (HF) or as a worded question (HCN), so no hazardous substance is shown in a school cup. No new plates needed. No human figures.
design.transitionPlan: Two calorimeter plates open with amber readouts and a ΔH bar chart with a dashed −57 line; two particle lenses compare a strong and a weak acid, then the weak-acid lens enlarges as hydroxide streams in and the "whole molecules left" counter falls to 0; the enthalpy staircase draws with a step 1 arrow whose direction is not yet set; the energy ledger draws for bond breaking against hydration; the staircase returns for each case and changes only its step 1 arrow (ethanoic acid, HF, ammonia); the Ka cards and a crossed chip close the strength point; the memory aid writes large; each attempt clears the board and its feedback underlines the givens as they are used; the decision rule card and next chip close; scene crossfade with settle.
